clue.text: Ruskin's architectural Seven

parts.note: John Ruskin's 1849 book on building names seven guiding principles, each pictured as a source of light

explanation.surface: A reference to the seven principles in a famous Victorian critic's book on architecture.
explanation.walkthrough: Ruskin's book is The Seven Lamps of Architecture; the clue is a general-knowledge prompt asking what the Seven were.
explanation.definitionFit: Ruskin titled his principles of building (Sacrifice, Truth, Power and so on) as lights guiding the architect.

clue.text: It's plain sailing for this

parts.note: read as sailing across a level plain, not as something easy

explanation.surface: Something for which everything goes smoothly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'plain sailing' means easy going, but here it is sailing over a plain: a wheeled craft with a sail runs on flat sand or land.
explanation.definitionFit: A wheeled vehicle with a sail is driven by the wind across beaches and flats.

clue.text: "Ends all our - -long love in this ?" (Bridges)

parts.note: a line from Robert Bridges with one word missing, used twice, which the solver supplies

explanation.surface: A quotation from the poet Robert Bridges with gaps to fill.
explanation.walkthrough: The same word fills both the dash and the question mark: a love of so long ending in this period of time.
explanation.definitionFit: The gap is a unit of time of about four weeks, filling both blanks in the line.

clue.text: Relish a process of time

definitions.meaning: something that adds flavour to food
the slow drying and maturing of timber over time

explanation.definitionFit: Salt and spice add flavour as a relish does, and timber is left to mature over months.

clue.text: Tough body material of a vehicle with lights on reversing to the end of the garage

parts.note: a car is a vehicle

indicators.note: reversing tells us the word for lights on is written backwards

parts.note: when the lights are on, the room is lit

indicators.note: to the end of points at the final stretch of the word garage, its last three letters

explanation.surface: A motoring description of a car backing into the garage with its headlamps on.
explanation.walkthrough: 'reversing' turns LIT into TIL, and 'to the end of' takes the closing AGE of 'garage'. The vehicle and garage suggest motoring, but the definition is anatomical.
explanation.definitionFit: Gristle, the firm flexible tissue at joints and in the nose and ears, is the tough material meant.

clue.text: A physics specialist who returns to the charge ?

definitions.text: A physics specialist who returns to the charge ?

parts.words: A physics specialist who returns to the charge ?
parts.note: physic means medicine, so the specialist dispenses remedies and comes back to what you are charged

explanation.surface: A scientist in physics who goes back on the attack.
explanation.walkthrough: 'physics' here is the old plural of physic, medicines, so this is a pharmacist; 'returns to the charge' plays on attacking again and on handing back change from the charge.
explanation.definitionFit: A pharmacist, who makes up and sells medicines (physic), is called this in Britain.

clue.text: Widows

parts.note: women whose husbands have died, using an old legal word for a survivor

explanation.definitionFit: An archaic term for a widow is one left behind by a dead husband, from Latin for left.

clue.text: A symbolic Scots ending-tough stuff !

indicators.note: ending asks for only the closing part of the emblem's name, dropping its start

parts.note: the thistle is the national emblem of Scotland

explanation.surface: A remark that Scots symbolism ends in something tough.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ending' keeps the end of THISTLE, dropping TH. Istle is a hard fibre from Mexican agave plants, used for cord and brushes.
explanation.definitionFit: Istle is a strong coarse plant fibre used for cordage, brushes and matting.

clue.text: Ay, it's true, that's what we are in for

annotationWithheld.why: Ay, it's true, that's what we are in for (9): AUSTERITY is an anagram of AY ITS TRUE, but no clue word signals the anagram; 'that's what we are in for' is all definition, so the op has no indicator
annotationWithheld.clue: Ay, it's true, that's what we are in for

clue.text: Asian treaty takes an excess of time

parts.note: E stands for East or Eastern, hence Asian
a pact is a treaty

explanation.surface: A treaty between Asian nations taking too long.
explanation.walkthrough: In the calendar this term counts the days by which the solar year exceeds twelve lunar months.
explanation.definitionFit: The epact is the number of days the solar year runs beyond twelve lunar months, an extra stretch of time.

clue.text: A type of excellence

parts.note: read both as a printer's type size and as a model of unrivalled excellence

explanation.surface: A phrase describing a paragon, something of supreme quality.
explanation.walkthrough: 'type' works twice: a paragon is a type of excellence, and printers once called a six-point typeface by this name.
explanation.definitionFit: The word means an unrivalled paragon and is also an old printing term for six-point type.

clue.text: The reverse of a good thing for the little contadina

indicators.note: The reverse of says the word for a good thing is written backwards

parts.note: an asset is a good thing to have

explanation.surface: A remark that the opposite of a benefit falls to a small peasant girl.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The reverse of' turns ASSET into TESSA, a contadina (Italian peasant girl) in Gilbert and Sullivan's The Gondoliers.
explanation.definitionFit: Tessa is one of the two peasant girls in Gilbert and Sullivan's operetta set in Venice.

clue.text: Turn the fodder to find your spectacles, brute

indicators.note: Turn asks for the word for fodder to be read backwards

parts.note: hay is animal fodder
two round lenses look like the letters OO

explanation.surface: An instruction to search the hay for lost glasses, addressed to a brute.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Turn' makes YAH from HAY; spectacles are drawn as OO. The brutish Yahoos come from Gulliver's Travels.
explanation.definitionFit: Swift's Yahoos are degraded humanlike beasts, so the word names a coarse, brutish person.

clue.text: Get right in, in builders' material for profit

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: Get right in tells us the letter for right goes inside the next piece

parts.note: cement is a builders' material

explanation.surface: A builder told to get something properly set in the cement for a profit.
explanation.walkthrough: The first 'in' is the container signal, putting R inside CEMENT; the second 'in' supplies its own letters in front.
explanation.definitionFit: An increment is a gain or increase, as profit is an addition to what one has.

clue.text: Car for the tea-fight

parts.note: cha is slang for tea
a riot is a violent disturbance or fight

explanation.surface: Asking which vehicle to take to a tea party.
explanation.walkthrough: A tea-fight is old slang for a tea party, but the hyphenated word splits into tea and fight. 'Car' is used in its poetic sense of a chariot.
explanation.definitionFit: In poetry a car is a chariot, as in the sun god's car crossing the sky.

clue.text: Sir, a turn of the tide's just general

parts.note: taken as written

indicators.note: a turn of the tide suggests change, so these letters are rearranged

parts.note: taken as written
the word tides, with the apostrophe ignored

explanation.surface: Addressing a knight about the tide turning, said to be just general.
explanation.walkthrough: 'turn of the' rearranges SIR, A and TIDES. Aristides the Just was an Athenian general and statesman.
explanation.definitionFit: The Athenian commander at Marathon was known as 'the Just' for his fairness.

clue.text: Missis is in the pink !

parts.note: read as a famous garden pink named after a Mrs, rather than a wife in good health

explanation.surface: A cheerful report that the wife is in good health.
explanation.walkthrough: 'in the pink' means healthy, but here the Missis is a pink: Mrs Sinkins is a well-known old white garden pink (dianthus).
explanation.definitionFit: The garden pink called Mrs Sinkins is named after the wife of a Slough workhouse master.

clue.text: U.s. name for 18th-century Bath ?

parts.note: Beau Nash ruled Bath society in the 1700s, so it might be called his town, as an American city is named

explanation.surface: Asking what Americans would call the Georgian spa town.
explanation.walkthrough: Beau Nash was master of ceremonies at Bath, England's fashionable spa, in the 18th century; adding -ville, the American town ending, gives the Tennessee city.
explanation.definitionFit: The capital of Tennessee combines a surname with -ville, the common American suffix for a town.

clue.text: In defence of which " the Spanish maid, aroused, Hangs on the willow her unstrung guitar"

definitions.text: In defence of which " the Spanish maid, aroused, Hangs on the willow her unstrung guitar"

parts.words: In defence of which " the Spanish maid, aroused, Hangs on the willow her unstrung guitar"
parts.note: lines from Byron's Childe Harold about a Spanish girl who joined the defence of her city

explanation.surface: Byron's picture of a Spanish girl putting away music for war.
explanation.walkthrough: Byron praises the Maid of Saragossa, Agustina, who manned the guns when the French besieged the city in 1808.
explanation.definitionFit: The Spanish city of Zaragoza, besieged by the French in the Peninsular War, is the setting of Byron's lines.

clue.text: Sharp reminders

parts.note: read as sudden pangs of pain that remind one of an ailment or a regret

explanation.surface: Pointed prompts that something must not be forgotten.
explanation.definitionFit: Sudden pangs, of pain or of conscience, are sharp reminders of a hurt or a fault.

clue.text: Show a clean pair of heels ? Quite the opposite effect

definitions.text: Show a clean pair of heels ? Quite the opposite effect

parts.words: Show a clean pair of heels ? Quite the opposite effect
parts.note: running away shows the heels, but this treatment leaves the head, the opposite end, clean

explanation.surface: A remark about escaping quickly, with a twist.
explanation.walkthrough: To show a clean pair of heels is to run away; this hair wash cleans the other end of a person.
explanation.definitionFit: Hair washing liquid cleans the head, the end of the body opposite the heels.

clue.text: A trying sort

parts.note: read as one whose job is to try or test metals, not an irritating person

explanation.surface: A description of an annoying, tiresome person.
explanation.walkthrough: 'trying' looks like 'irritating', but it means testing: to assay is to try the purity of a metal.
explanation.definitionFit: This person tests ores and metals for their content, to try them in the old sense.

clue.text: A place of ups and downs that's flat

definitions.text: A place of ups and downs that's flat

parts.words: A place of ups and downs that's flat
parts.note: read as aircraft taking off and landing at a level field

explanation.surface: A paradox about somewhere both hilly and level.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ups and downs' suggests hills, but here planes go up and come down on flat ground.
explanation.definitionFit: Aircraft take off and land at this level site, so it sees constant ups and downs.

clue.text: Sitz ?

parts.note: the German word for seat, familiar from the hip bath called a sitz-bath, is read as seat plus bath

explanation.surface: A one-word question in German.
explanation.walkthrough: A sitz-bath is a hip bath; reversing the idea, a seat linked with Bath gives the wheeled invalid chair named after the spa town.
explanation.definitionFit: The hooded wheeled chair for invalids took its name from the spa town where it was common, and Sitz is German for seat.

clue.text: Stripped, was blushful to a degree

parts.note: BA, Bachelor of Arts, is a university degree
to be blushful is to go red in the face

explanation.surface: Someone undressed and blushed deeply.
explanation.walkthrough: 'to a degree' reads as 'somewhat', but the degree is a university one, and blushing is a colour.
explanation.definitionFit: Bared means uncovered or laid naked, as stripped skin is.

clue.text: Pupil of Antisthenes

parts.note: Antisthenes, a follower of Socrates, founded a Greek school of philosophy scorning wealth and convention

explanation.surface: A follower of a Greek philosopher.
explanation.definitionFit: Members of the school founded by Antisthenes rejected convention, and the word now means a sneering doubter.

clue.text: I leave Ivy with a mixed drink trying to be winning

indicators.note: I leave Ivy says the letter I goes out of the name

parts.note: taken as written
taken as written

indicators.note: mixed says the letters of the drink are shuffled

parts.note: gin is a drink

explanation.surface: Someone abandons Ivy over cocktails while trying to win.
explanation.walkthrough: 'I leave' takes I out of IVY to leave VY; 'mixed' turns GIN into ING.
explanation.definitionFit: Vying means competing, striving to come out on top.

clue.text: One of the blinkers of Russian reading

definitions.text: One of the blinkers of Russian reading

parts.words: One of the blinkers of Russian reading
parts.note: a famous Russian novel whose title names a fool, so a blinkered or foolish man

explanation.surface: A restricted view of Russian literature.
explanation.walkthrough: Dostoevsky's novel The Idiot is staple Russian reading; 'blinkers' hints at a fool who cannot see.
explanation.definitionFit: Dostoevsky's novel is titled after a simpleton, a fool in common speech.

clue.text: Sappers take tribal city for fortification

parts.note: RE, the Royal Engineers, are the sappers of the British Army
Dan was the city of the Israelite tribe of Dan, at the northern limit of the land

explanation.surface: Army engineers capturing a tribe's city to build a fort.
explanation.walkthrough: In the phrase 'from Dan to Beersheba', Dan is the northern city named for its tribe.
explanation.definitionFit: A redan is a field work with two faces forming a salient angle toward the enemy.

clue.text: States publicly one is in favour of the demands

parts.note: a pro is one who is in favour, as in pros and cons
claims are demands

explanation.surface: Someone announces support for a set of demands.
explanation.definitionFit: To proclaim is to announce or declare openly, as a herald does.

clue.text: Don't cast this till you have a washing-up machine !

definitions.text: Don't cast this till you have a washing-up machine !

parts.words: Don't cast this till you have a washing-up machine !
parts.note: a twist on the saying about not casting a clout till May is out, with the clout now a kitchen rag

explanation.surface: Advice not to throw away a household item until a dishwasher arrives.
explanation.walkthrough: The proverb 'Ne'er cast a clout till May be out' warns against shedding clothes early; clout also means a cloth, here one used for dishes.
explanation.definitionFit: This is an old word for a dishcloth, clout being dialect for a rag or cloth.

clue.text: There is a bonus in the next raffle

indicators.note: in the next raffle says the letters lie inside those two words

explanation.surface: Good news that a prize is on offer at the next raffle.
explanation.definitionFit: Something additional, such as a bonus, is more than the usual amount.
